[tool: bash]
I wrote `polyglot/main.rs`. It compiles with both `rustc` and `g++ -x c++`, and both programs printed the same answers when I ran them for N = 0, 1, 2, 3, 10, 50 and 100:

| N | Output |
|---|---|

| 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 |
| 3 | 3 |
| 10 | 89 |
| 50 | 20365011074 |
| 100 | 573147844013817084101 |

**How it works:** the trick is that Rust lets block comments nest and C++ doesn't.
- The file starts with `/* /* */`. C++ treats that as one complete comment and goes on to read the C++ code. Rust sees two comments opened and only one closed, so it skips everything up to a later `// */`.
- After the C++ `main`, an `#if 0` hides the Rust code from C++. At the end of the file, a second `/* /* */` … `#endif` / `// */` pair hides the `#endif` from Rust, using the same nesting rule.

Both versions do the addition in base 10⁹ chunks, so large N gives the exact answer instead of overflowing 64-bit integers. If N is missing or can't be read as a number, both print f(0) = 1.

Running the test also left the compiled binaries `polyglot/main` and `polyglot/cmain` in the directory.
